How this preview works

1Look from the transmitter

The antenna stands 3 m above the ground. From there the page casts 720 rays and samples the terrain every metre along each ray, up to 363 m.

2Scan for the horizon

Along each ray it keeps the highest elevation angle seen so far. A receiver 1 m above the ground that sits below this horizon is in shadow. The dotted line on the map is the shadow edge.

3Add the losses

Free-space loss on the 3D distance, plus a knife-edge term for the strongest obstacle on the path. Received power is 20 dBm minus the path loss.

4Next: the trained RayNet

The network will learn a correction on top of this estimate from 25,720 ray-traced maps per band. It will run in this page with ONNX Runtime Web, in about the same time.

This preview is a physics estimate, not the trained model. In the ray tracer that made the training data, diffraction is turned off. So real shadows behind crater rims are usually darker than shown here. Learning that difference is the network's job.

Tile256 m × 256 m, 1 m per pixel
Transmitter20 dBm, isotropic, 3 m above terrain
Receiverisotropic, 1 m above terrain
Bands415 MHz (λ = 0.72 m) · 5.775 GHz (λ = 5.2 cm)
Free-space loss20·log10(d) + 20·log10(f) − 147.55 dB
Knife-edgeJ(ν) = 6.9 + 20·log10(√((ν−0.1)²+1) + ν − 0.1), ν > −0.78
TerrainsGenerated with LunarTerrainGenerator, the same open generator used for the training data
